In June 2024, a 17-year-old vocational fashion-design student placed twelfth in the first round of Alibaba's global math competition, beating gold medal Olympians. Within a day, her home county in China was using her to advertise its pig's feet. Jiang Ping told a Beijing newspaper that she taught herself university-level math, partly from an English-language textbook on partial differential equations, using a phone translation tool and a pocket dictionary. She scored 93 in the first round of the competition, qualifying for the final round with 800 other contestants. Her region's tourism bureau posted a video saying "Huai'an isn't big, but it makes legends." A businessman gave her father 5,000 yuan in cash, about $700, and another man measured the dirt road in front of her house, offering to pay to have it paved. Then the scrutiny began. Viewers paused frames of Alibaba's promotional video about her and noticed mistakes in the formulas she had written on a blackboard behind her: mistakes that the holder of such a high score would not make, such as the Greek letter sigma written as a slash and a two. Alibaba quietly took the word "genius" out of the video's title. The competition round she excelled in was 48 hours long, conducted over the internet. It was open book, taken at home, and unsupervised. The only rule was that competitors were not allowed to discuss the problems with others. Her math teacher, Wang Runqiu, took the contest too, and placed 125th. The final round was closed book, and ultimately neither teacher nor student won a prize. Then, in November, Alibaba revealed that the teacher had helped her in the first round, breaking the no-discussion rule, and apologized for failing to oversee the competition properly. His school gave him a formal warning talk. In China, around one in three students who starts high school gets diverted to a vocational school, based on an exam they take when they are 15. Jiang did well enough in that exam to go to a top local high school, but opted for a vocational school instead. Her story told all the families whose child was being streamed onto a vocational path that the exam you take when you are 15 doesn't decide everything. That's why her home county and Alibaba were so keen to spread her name before they had bothered to look into a test she took unsupervised at home. And when it blew up, the teacher was given a talk. But in China, the scandal is known as the Jiang Ping affair, named after a 17-year-old girl.
